newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Guilder seen holding key to Dutch rate outlook.
newsitem.headline: Guilder seen holding key to Dutch rate outlook.

text.p: Two leading authorities have fuelled speculation of a further tightening of Dutch monetary policy, but the guilder would need to weaken again to prompt a further increase in official interest rates, analysts said.
Some forecasters said official rates may rise to the level of those in Germany this year and one economist even expects them to exceed German rates for the first time in six years.
"There's a very good chance that rates will move higher and above Germany in the course of this year," said J.P. Morgan economist Ellen van der Gulik.
In the Dutch central bank's annual report issued in April, president Wim Duisenberg said the Dutch economy was "beginning to show signs of monetary exuberance".
He cited the 15 percent domestic money growth in 1996, fuelled by mortgage loans as house prices increased strongly and interest rates remained low.
Shortly thereafter, the International Monetary Fund said action may be needed to contain relatively buoyant Dutch demand.
Van der Gulik said Dutch consumers were on a spending spree, with low interest rates and rising asset prices giving an extra kick to consumption.
She expected the Dutch special advances rate to rise to 3.50 percent, or 50 basis points over its German equivalent, the repo rate, by the end of 1997.
The special advances rate, at 2.90 percent, is now 10 basis points below the repo.
She said the timing of interest rate hikes would depend on the guilder exchange rate against the German mark, adding that she expected the guilder to weaken.
Among the reasons were her expectation that Dutch inflation would be 100 basis points higher than German inflation by the end of this year, compared with 50 basis points in March.
The continuing diversification by Dutch investors out of Dutch assets into foreign assets could also have an impact.
"If you see a massive outflow, that would undermine the guilder," van der Gulik said.
Rabobank International said in a research report that Dutch monetary conditions were too loose and that Duisenberg had clearly indicated a rate hike would be warranted.

It said a rise in Dutch inflation in the late spring and summer might push the mark up to its central parity rate of 1.12673 guilders, triggering a 10 basis point hike in the special advances rate, which sets the tone for money rates.
The mark was trading at 1.1251 guilders at 0905 GMT.
In March, the Dutch central bank increased official rates twice in two weeks to support the guilder which had slipped to levels of around 1.1260 versus the mark.
Rabobank fixed interest analyst Niels Kortleve said the warnings from Duisenberg and the IMF had not affected the market to date.
But he added: "In the next few months, or maybe weeks, the topic of Dutch central bank hikes will be back in the market."
But Gerlof de Vrij of ABN AMRO did not see a large risk to Dutch inflation from high economic growth because wage increases were being kept low.
He did not expect the central bank to hike interest rates this year as the guilder was still below its parity rate.

MeesPierson economist Aline Schuiling said the guilder would not weaken enough to force the Dutch central bank to lift the special advances rate, adding that it would remain at a 10 basis point discount to the German repo rate this year.
"I think they will try to keep it that way," she said.
She said the Netherlands' current account surplus, compared with Germany's recurring deficit, was sufficient to support the Dutch currency.
